doc.title: Warren Smith interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, March 17, 2018

chapter: Max Roach, M'Boom and Sun Ra
title: Max Roach's temperament and the Beehive story with Clifford Brown
summary: Roach was emotionally open and volatile; at the Beehive in Chicago he lowered his volume when Clifford Brown whispered to him.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Playing with Miles Davis: joining, sessions and the band

blocks.x: Wow. You’ve worked with some memorable musicians and artists over the years. And I believe you said you were talking about Max Roach. And he had an ego you said.

Oh man, that was an education in itself. I mean here’s a person who had a variation from piano to quadruple forte, even emotionally. You know I mean he could be the most kindest, most loving person in the world, gentle. But there were times when you could

see him gritting his teeth and chewing his jaws and you could see where something was about to implode and he could erupt. You know he and I, I mean I guess maybe I’m an amateur psychologist. I like to read people. And I usually can avoid problems by anticipating somebody’s emotions. But I remember a couple of times he and I got into shouting matches about something. And something in me would never let me back down. You know, and we wound up being able to get along really well with each other because of that. But I mean now here’s a musical genius but he was open, but he was also emotionally open and that could go either way you know what I mean? Being emotionally open he is vulnerable. So certain things could excite him, you know, or make him angry, and he might react. If he’s got the drumset he can react with that. But if the drumset is not there you might be a percussion instrument. But I mean he was, the first music that I heard I was watching Max Roach and listening to him.

Yeah. Oh we had his records you know. I mean he was like a teenager himself when I first heard him, when he first started playing all these things. But the first time I heard him — I’ll show you how sensitive he was — I went to a club in Chicago called the Beehive. And a friend of mine was there. He was working with Clifford Brown. And we went and heard him and Clifford was watching the audience when he wasn’t — Max was playing, and Max was playing kind of loud. And this friend of mine, I’m watching the stage all the time. And he says, “Man, Max Roach is playing too loud.” And Clifford read his lips. And he turned around and I said oh shit, something’s gonna — he turned around and he whispered something in Max’s ear, and Max diminished his volume. He responded to it. He had that kind of respect for Clifford Brown. He wouldn’t have accepted that from me necessarily, or from another audience member. But this is the kind of nuances that you deal with, with an artist of this capability and breadth of expression I guess you know. It could go any way. But it’s a great lesson to observe.
